extracted.intended_audience: authors, peer reviewers, editors, publishers, and journal owners involved in medical/biomedical journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: ICMJE Recommendations for conduct, reporting, editing, and publication of scholarly work in medical journals — guidance for preparing manuscripts, disclosing relationships, peer review, editorial responsibilities, and use of AI. Intended to be used by those submitting to or operating medical journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICMJE authorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE recommends that authorship be based on the following 4 criteria: 1. Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data for the work; AND 2. Drafting the work or reviewing it critically for important intellectual content; AND 3. Final approval of the version to be published; AND 4. Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work in ensuring that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work are appropriately investigated and resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All those designated as authors should meet all four criteria, and all who meet the four criteria should be identified as authors. Criteria are not to be used to deny opportunities to meet criterion #2 or #3. Authors should be able to identify which co-authors are responsible for specific parts and have confidence in co-authors' integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding author responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding author is the one individual who takes primary responsibility for communication with the journal during the manuscript submission, peer-review, and publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically ensures administrative requirements (authorship details, ethics approval, trial registration, disclosures) are completed, is available throughout submission and after publication to respond to editorial queries, and may delegate duties to co-authors. Editors are recommended to send copies of all correspondence to all listed authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group authorship and byline reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When a large multi-author group has conducted the work, the group ideally should decide who will be an author before the work is started and confirm who is an author before submitting the manuscript for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponding author should specify group name and clearly identify group members who can take credit and responsibility as authors. MEDLINE lists as authors whichever names appear on the byline; if a group name is used, individual names must be clearly located elsewhere in the paper with indication whether they are authors or collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-author contributors and acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors who meet fewer than all 4 authorship criteria should not be listed as authors but should be acknowledged, with their contributions specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of activities that alone do not qualify for authorship: acquisition of funding, general supervision, administrative support, writing assistance, technical or language editing, and proofreading. Require written permission from acknowledged individuals because acknowledgment may imply endorsement. Report use of AI for writing assistance in the acknowledgment section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributorship policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are strongly encouraged to develop and implement a contributorship policy to remove ambiguity surrounding contributions and distinguish authors from other contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such policies should require and publish information about the contributions of each person named as participating in a submitted study, at least for original research, while recognizing that criteria about quantity/quality of contribution remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of financial and non-financial relationships and activities, and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose all relationships and activities that might bias or be seen to bias their work when they submit a manuscript of any type or format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent disclosures help readers judge pertinence of relationships. Financial relationships (employment, consultancies, stock, honoraria, patents, paid testimony) are most easily identifiable, but non-financial interests (personal relationships, rivalries, academic competition, intellectual beliefs) may also represent conflicts. Purposeful failure to report specified relationships is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standardized disclosure form and reporting relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICMJE has developed a Disclosure Form to facilitate and standardize authors' disclosures; ICMJE member journals require its use and others are encouraged to adopt it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles should be published with statements or supporting documents declaring authors' relationships and activities; sources of support for the work including sponsor names and explanations of their role; and whether authors had access to the study data, with explanation of nature and extent of access. Editors may request signed statements (e.g., 'I had full access to all of the data...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must avoid agreements that limit access or academic freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must avoid entering into agreements with study sponsors that interfere with authors' access to all of the study's data or that interfere with their ability to analyze, interpret, and publish manuscripts independently when and where they choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that dictate where authors may publish violate academic freedom. Authors may be required to provide the journal with sponsor agreements in confidence. Nondisclosure of relationships or restrictive agreements can be grounds for corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of predatory or pseudo-journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have a responsibility to evaluate the integrity, history, practices, and reputation of the journals to which they submit manuscripts and to avoid submitting to journals that function as 'predatory' or 'pseudo-journals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predatory journals often accept almost all submissions, charge fees, falsely claim peer review or memberships, and may inform authors of fees only after acceptance. Authors should also avoid citing articles from such journals and consult guidance (WAME etc.) to identify characteristics of reputable journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of manuscripts and review materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts submitted to journals are privileged communications that are authors' private, confidential property; editors and reviewers must keep manuscript information strictly confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must not share manuscript status, content, reviewer criticisms, or fate with anyone other than authors and reviewers. Reviewers must not appropriate ideas, retain manuscripts for personal use, or publicly discuss the work. AI processing of manuscripts may violate confidentiality; uploading manuscripts into AI systems where confidentiality cannot be assured is prohibited without explicit permission. Journals should disclose retention practices and keep published submission records for at least three years (possibly longer based on local regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and responsiveness of journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should ensure timely processing of manuscripts with the resources available, and respond to authors' requests about manuscript status in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors intend to publish a manuscript, they should attempt timely publication or negotiate planned delays with authors. If a journal has no intention to proceed, it should reject as soon as possible. Withdrawal requests by authors in good faith should be honored even without confirmation from the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the critical assessment of manuscripts by experts and the journal is responsible for systems to select appropriate reviewers and provide them access to all relevant materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should ensure reviewer comments are assessed in context of declared relationships. Journals should publish a clear, transparent description of their peer-review process for all manuscript types. Journals are not obligated to send manuscripts for review nor to follow reviewer recommendations; editors have ultimate responsibility for content selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and transparency of protocols, statistical plans, and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are encouraged to review research protocols, statistical analysis plans, and contracts; authors should be encouraged to make such documents publicly available at or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals may require posting of these documents as a condition of acceptance. Requirements for independent data analysis and public data availability vary by journal. ICMJE believes investigators have a duty to maintain primary data and analytic procedures for at least 10 years and encourages preservation in a data repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial integrity in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions should be based on the relevance of a manuscript to the journal and on the manuscript's originality, quality, and contribution to evidence about important questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should not be influenced by commercial interests, personal relationships, agendas, or results (including negative or inconclusive findings). Journals should state their appeals process and have a system for responding to appeals and complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and inclusion in publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should seek to engage a broad and diverse array of authors, reviewers, editorial staff, editorial board members, and readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing images of people, avoid those that depict individuals in distress or could perpetuate bias or stereotypes; consider whether an image is necessary for understanding the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible use of journal metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal impact factor is widely misused; journals should reduce emphasis on impact factor as a single measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a range of article and journal metrics relevant to readers and authors rather than relying solely on impact factor as a proxy for research or researcher quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must keep manuscripts and their information strictly confidential, must not appropriate authors' ideas, must destroy copies after review, and must disclose relationships or activities that could bias their evaluation and recuse if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers who seek assistance from trainees or colleagues should acknowledge their contributions in submitted comments. Reviewers must request permission before using AI technologies to facilitate reviews and should not upload manuscripts into AI systems where confidentiality cannot be assured. Reviews should be submitted promptly and be constructive, honest, and polite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal owners' responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal owners should explicitly state governance and relationship to owners and provide editors with a contract stating rights, duties, authority, and mechanisms for resolving conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners are responsible for appointing and dismissing editors, but dismissals should be only for substantial reasons (scientific misconduct, disagreement with long-term editorial direction, inadequate performance, inappropriate behavior) and based on evaluation by an independent panel rather than a small executive group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors-in-chief should have full authority over editorial content and timing of publication; owners should not interfere in evaluation, selection, scheduling, or editing of individual articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should base decisions on validity and importance to readers, be free to express critical views without fear of retribution, have final say on advertisements and use of journal brand, have direct access to highest level of ownership, and be supported with legal advice and insurance when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of research participants and research ethics approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should ensure planning, conduct, and reporting of human research are in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration (revised 2024) and seek approval from an independent review body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide documentation when requested; if doubt exists about adherence, authors must explain rationale and show the review body approved doubtful aspects. Approval does not preclude editors' judgment on appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent for identifiable patient information
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients have a right to privacy that should not be violated without informed consent; identifying information should not be published unless essential and written informed consent is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informed consent for publication requires that an identifiable patient be shown the manuscript to be published. Authors should disclose to patients that identifiable material may be available on the Internet and in print. Consent should be written and archived per local regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting guidelines for specific study types
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should consult guidelines for reporting specific study types (e.g., CONSORT for randomized trials) when preparing manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE encourages using EQUATOR Network resources and following journal-specific instructions; journals may require submission checklists such as CONSORT with the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript structure and section-specific standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should include standard sections (Title Page, Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, References, Tables, Illustrations) organized according to general principles and journal instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods should detail participant selection and description, data collection and measurements, and statistics. Discussion should clearly state principal findings, strengths and limitations, interpretation, and conclusions; label new hypotheses clearly. Follow journal-specific guidance for format and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: References — general considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide direct references to original research sources whenever possible; references should be made to published articles rather than abstracts, and avoid citing articles from predatory journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preprints are cited, clearly indicate they are preprints. Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable. Authors must verify references (e.g., via PubMed) and ensure retracted articles are not cited except when referring to the retraction. Include persistent identifiers for datasets used.

rubrics_metrics.name: References — style and format
rubrics_metrics.description: References should follow NLM's Sample References and the Citing Medicine guidance; references numbered consecutively in order first mentioned, with journal titles abbreviated per MEDLINE standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult the target journal's instructions for exact reference formats for electronic sources and other media; sequence for citations in text, tables, and legends must be consistent with first mention order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables — presentation and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tables according to specific journal requirements; number tables consecutively in order of first citation and supply a short but self-explanatory title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place explanatory material in footnotes rather than headings, explain nonstandard abbreviations, identify statistical measures of variation, obtain permission for reproduced data, and provide extensive backup tables as supplementary electronic material with statement in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and illustrations — technical and ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital images should be submitted in suitable format and high resolution; photomicrographs require internal scale markers; figures should be self-explanatory with legends on separate pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters/numbers must remain legible when reduced; explain symbols/arrows in legends; obtain written permission to reproduce previously published figures irrespective of authorship; for clinical images, consider dignity and consent issues and ensure before-and-after images are comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurements of length, height, weight, and volume should be reported in metric units (meter, kilogram, liter) or their decimal multiples; temperatures in degrees Celsius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals vary for hematologic and chemistry units; authors should report laboratory information in both local and International System of Units (SI) when appropriate and consult journal instructions. Editors may request alternative or non-SI units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only standard abbreviations and avoid nonstandard abbreviations; avoid abbreviations in the manuscript title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out the term followed by the abbreviation in parentheses on first mention (unless a standard unit). Explain all nonstandard abbreviations in footnotes or legend as required by the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter and submission documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be accompanied by a cover letter or completed submission form including statements about redundant publication, disclosures, authorship, contact information, prior submissions, and permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full statement about previous reports that might be redundant, copies of such material, statements of financial or other relationships if not in the manuscript, authorship confirmation that all authors meet requirements, contact for proofs, previous editor/reviewer comments and responses (if previously submitted), permissions for reproduced material, and any presubmission checklists requested by the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in publishing — general
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors, reviewers, and editors/publishers should adhere to principles: do not list AI or AI-assisted technologies as an author; humans are responsible for accuracy, validity, and originality; disclose use of AI; and avoid uploading submissions to AI systems where confidentiality cannot be assured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AI can generate authoritative-sounding but incorrect or biased output, users must check accuracy, ensure proper attribution and permissions, and disclose which tools were used and for what purpose. Journals should have explicit policies covering AI use and inform editors, reviewers, and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI by authors — disclosure and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should require authors to disclose at submission whether they used AI-assisted technologies in producing submitted work and describe how they used it (in cover letter and appropriate manuscript section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI used for writing assistance, describe in acknowledgments; if used for data collection, analysis, or figure generation, describe in Methods. Chatbots should not be listed as authors or cited as authors. Authors must ensure there is no plagiarism in AI-generated text or images and must provide appropriate attribution for quoted material. Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable. Nondisclosure may be construed as misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI by reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must adhere to the journal's stated policy on AI use or request permission prior to using AI technology to facilitate review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reviewers must maintain confidentiality, uploading manuscripts to AI systems where confidentiality can't be assured is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the journal. Reviewers who use AI should disclose its use to the journal and ensure AI-generated content is valid and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' role in ensuring responsible use of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should query authors about AI use, require disclosure, develop and publicize journal policies on AI, and avoid uploading submitted manuscripts to AI systems where confidentiality cannot be assured without authors' permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should consider that use of AI for copy-editing or production should be disclosed to authors. Editors are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and validity of AI-generated ancillary content (podcasts, patient summaries, educational questions), and should be vigilant about undisclosed AI use by authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and handling of manuscript records
rubrics_metrics.description: When a manuscript is rejected, it is best practice for journals to delete copies from editorial systems unless retention is required by local regulations; when published, journals should keep copies of original submissions, reviews, revisions, and correspondence for at least three years and possibly in perpetuity depending on local regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals that retain copies of rejected manuscripts should disclose the practice in their Information for Authors. Requests from third parties to use manuscripts and reviews for legal proceedings should generally be refused; editors should notify authors if confidentiality must be breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling authorship disputes and changes after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The individuals who conduct the work are responsible for identifying who meets authorship criteria; the order of authorship is decided collectively by the author group, not editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors request removal or addition of an author after submission or publication, editors should seek explanation and a signed statement of agreement for the change from all authors and from the author to be removed or added. If agreement cannot be reached, the institutions where the work was performed should investigate — not the journal editor.
